subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Endogenous factors shaping a place's character are best described as those that are:
options: External flows arriving from elsewhere
Determined entirely by national government
Always physical rather than human
Internal characteristics originating within the place itself
questions.explain: Endogenous factors are internal characteristics of a place, such as its physical geography, land use, built environment and demographics.

questions.q: Place character can change over time mainly because of changes in:
options: Connections, flows and the relationships a place has with other places
Nothing; place character is permanent
The fixed coordinates of the location
The colour of the sky only
questions.explain: Places are dynamic and their character shifts as flows of people, money, ideas and investment change over time.

questions.q: Why do many former industrial places require regeneration?
options: They have too many high-paid jobs
They have excessive inward investment
Their populations are growing too rapidly
Deindustrialisation has caused unemployment, dereliction and social decline
questions.explain: Deindustrialisation often leaves behind unemployment, derelict land and social problems that regeneration seeks to address.

questions.q: A formal representation of a place is best illustrated by:
options: Census data and Ordnance Survey maps
A film depicting local life
A novel set in the town
A piece of graffiti art
questions.explain: Formal representations are objective and often statistical, such as census data, official maps and government reports.

questions.q: A place described as a 'palimpsest' is one that:
options: Has a single, unchanging use
Shows layers of past developments still visible in its present landscape
Is entirely underwater
Has no history at all
questions.explain: A palimpsest describes how successive layers of past land use and development remain partly visible in the present landscape.

questions.q: A common social cost of gentrification is:
options: A reduction in cafes and independent shops
Total loss of investment in the area
Displacement of long-standing, lower-income communities
Falling house prices for all
questions.explain: As property values rise, original lower-income residents are often priced out and displaced from gentrifying areas.

questions.q: In the study of place, what does the term 'locale' refer to?
options: The setting and material structures in which social relations are conducted
The subjective feelings people attach to a place
The flows of people into and out of a place
The absolute coordinates of a place
questions.explain: Locale refers to the actual setting and material structures where everyday activities and social relations take place.

questions.q: Which factor is most clearly an endogenous influence on a town's character?
options: International tourism trends
The town's local building materials and topography
Global commodity prices
A new motorway built by national government to a distant city
questions.explain: Local physical features such as topography and building materials are internal, endogenous characteristics of the place.

questions.q: Place-marketing through hosting a major event such as a culture festival is intended to:
options: Raise a place's profile and attract investment and tourism
Reduce visitor numbers permanently
Demolish the historic core
Discourage media coverage
questions.explain: Hosting major events is a place-marketing strategy to boost profile, attract visitors and stimulate investment.

questions.q: Property-led regeneration of the 1980s London Docklands was led principally by:
options: An overseas charity alone
A community housing cooperative
An Urban Development Corporation attracting private investment
A national farming union
questions.explain: The London Docklands Development Corporation used property-led, private-investment regeneration to transform a derelict industrial area.

questions.q: A place's 'location' is best described as:
options: The way it is portrayed in the media
The community living within it
The emotional meaning attached to it
Its position on a map, often expressed using coordinates
questions.explain: Location is the absolute position of a place, typically described using map coordinates such as latitude and longitude.

questions.q: An 'experienced place' differs from a 'media place' because an experienced place is:
options: One only ever seen on television or film
Necessarily an overseas location
Always more accurately represented
One a person has visited or lived in first-hand
questions.explain: Experienced places are those a person has direct, lived contact with, whereas media places are known only second-hand through representation.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the relational concept of place?
options: Place identity is fixed at the moment of settlement
Place is defined only by its physical soil type
Places exist in complete isolation
A place's identity is partly shaped by its connections and relationships with other places
questions.explain: A relational view sees place identity as produced through networks and connections with other places, not as self-contained.

questions.q: Which best distinguishes a 'near place' from a 'far place'?
options: Near places exist; far places are imaginary
Near places are richer; far places are poorer
Near places feel geographically and emotionally close, while far places feel distant or alien
Near places are always rural; far places are always urban
questions.explain: Near and far refer to perceived closeness, both in physical distance and in emotional or cultural familiarity, not just kilometres.

questions.q: 'Place-marketing' (re-imaging) is best defined as:
options: The demolition of all old buildings
Promoting a positive image of a place to attract investment, residents or visitors
The mapping of a place using GIS
The compulsory purchase of derelict land
questions.explain: Place-marketing deliberately constructs a positive image of a place to attract investment, businesses, tourists and residents.

questions.q: Which of the following is a demographic measure of regeneration success?
options: The price of bus tickets only
The number of clouds overhead
The colour of new buildings
Changes in the age structure and population numbers of an area
questions.explain: Demographic indicators include changes in population size, age structure and the reduction of out-migration.

questions.q: Gentrification is best defined as the process by which:
options: Wealthier people move into and renovate a previously run-down area, often displacing poorer residents
An area's population falls to zero
Rural land is converted to farmland
Heavy industry returns to an inner-city district
questions.explain: Gentrification involves more affluent groups moving into and upgrading deprived areas, frequently displacing lower-income residents.

questions.q: A criticism of flagship, property-led regeneration is that it can:
options: Create benefits that fail to 'trickle down' to deprived local residents
Always benefit the original community equally
Prevent any new employment
Reduce land values everywhere
questions.explain: Such schemes are criticised because new wealth often does not trickle down to existing low-income communities.

questions.q: Which of the following would most likely be an 'outsider's' representation of a place?
options: A lifelong resident's memories
A community noticeboard
A national newspaper article written by a visiting journalist
A local resident's home video
questions.explain: Outsider representations come from those without a deep personal attachment, such as journalists, tourists or distant media.

questions.q: Government deprivation-led regeneration policy typically targets places with:
options: The highest average incomes
No housing at all
High scores on the Index of Multiple Deprivation
The lowest levels of multiple deprivation
questions.explain: Regeneration is often directed at areas scoring highly for multiple deprivation, indicating concentrated social and economic problems.

questions.q: An 'insider' perspective on a place is characterised by:
options: Treating the place purely as a tourist destination
Knowing only the formal statistical data about it
Viewing the place only through media representations
A sense of belonging, familiarity and identity with the place
questions.explain: An insider feels they belong to a place and experiences it as familiar, holding an identity bound up with it.

questions.q: How might the success of a regeneration scheme be measured economically?
options: By counting the number of pigeons
Through changes in employment rates and average household income
By measuring annual rainfall
By the number of road signs replaced
questions.explain: Economic success indicators include changes in employment, income levels, business start-ups and inward investment.

questions.q: Rebranding a place primarily aims to:
options: Reduce the resident population permanently
Change perceptions and reposition a place to reverse decline
Increase the area's natural hazard risk
Discourage all forms of in-migration
questions.explain: Rebranding seeks to change how a place is perceived and experienced, often to reverse economic or social decline.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of an exogenous factor influencing a place?
options: Inward migration and external investment flows
The age of the housing stock
The street layout of the town centre
The local geology and relief
questions.explain: Exogenous factors are external influences such as migration, money flows and the relationships a place has with other places.

questions.q: The 'lived experience' of a place refers to:
options: The day-to-day reality and meaning of a place for those who inhabit it
The official tourism brochure
The geological history of the bedrock
The international export figures
questions.explain: Lived experience captures how people actually use, understand and give meaning to the places of their everyday lives.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines 'sense of place'?
options: The geographical grid reference of a location
The total economic output of an area
The subjective and emotional attachment people have to a place
The transport links connecting a place to others
questions.explain: Sense of place is the personal, subjective and emotional meaning that individuals or groups attach to a place.

questions.q: In regeneration, which group is best described as a 'player' or stakeholder?
options: Local councils, developers, residents and businesses with an interest in the outcome
Only tourists passing through
Solely overseas governments
Only the national weather service
questions.explain: Players or stakeholders are individuals and groups with an interest in regeneration, including government, developers, businesses and communities.

questions.q: Which of the following is an informal representation of a place?
options: A song or poem written about the place
Government population statistics
An Ordnance Survey map
A geological survey
questions.explain: Informal representations are subjective and creative, such as art, photography, poetry, music and film.

questions.q: A 'flagship' regeneration scheme is one that:
options: Removes all retail from an area
Avoids any private investment
Relies only on small-scale community gardens
Uses a single large, prestigious project to act as a catalyst for wider renewal
questions.explain: Flagship developments are large, iconic projects intended to spark confidence and trigger further investment in an area.

questions.q: Studentification, a form of changing place character, refers to:
options: A fall in the number of young people
The conversion of cities into farmland
The concentration of student populations transforming the character of urban neighbourhoods
The closure of all universities in a region
questions.explain: Studentification occurs when large student populations change the social, economic and physical character of neighbourhoods near universities.
